title: Cascade degrade patterns and SLA playbook
content:
Overview

Quick working notes on a cascade-style degradation approach for regional routing, control-plane policy, and model-variant selection. Goal: keep client-facing SLOs predictable while minimizing cost and avoiding hard failures when capacity or model quality issues occur. This is a living doc — early sketches, heuristics, and runbook fragments for upcoming spike.

Why cascade degradation?
- We want monotonic tradeoffs: as load or failures increase, move along a deterministic sequence of cheaper/faster options rather than a binary on/off switch.
- Predictability for clients and observability for us: each rung has clear cost/latency/quality bounds.
- Easier reasoning about fallthroughs in multi-region deployments and hybrid dedicated/hosted capacity.

Principles and constraints
- SLOs map to two axes: perceived latency (p95/p99) and minimum quality (automated eval score threshold).
- Degradation steps must be reversible and testable in isolation.
- Control-plane should make deterministic decisions based on policy inputs: capacity, region, model-health signals, and client tier.
- Route early (edge) where possible to avoid excess cross-region cost; fall back to central policies only when necessary.

Key vocabulary (for consistency)
- Rung: a discrete degradation step (e.g., full-model in-region -> distill in-region -> quantized in-region -> cached-response -> region-fallback -> best-effort async).
- Degrade Ladder: ordered list of rungs used for decisioning.
- Overflow: intentional routing of requests to another region when local capacity is constrained.
- Control-plane policy: JSON-style set of rules evaluated by policy engine.

Example degrade ladder (customer-facing, ordered fastest/most-accurate -> slowest/cheapest):
1) prod-primary: full-precision model (fp16/amp) pinned version, KV warm cache, preferred region.
2) prod-distill: distilled model family (smaller decoder layers) with similar prompts.
3) prod-int8: quantized variant optimized for throughput.
4) cached-prefix: prefix cache hit -> respond from cached KV (low-latency).
5) regional-overflow: route to sibling region with same rung available.
6) degraded-mode-async: enqueue for background processing and return a deterministic placeholder.

Routing & control-plane heuristics
- Inputs to policy: current capacity usage (% GPU alloc), queue length, p95 latency, model eval error rate, region health flags, customer tier override.
- Priority scoring: combine inputs into a score. Score buckets map to rungs. E.g., score < .7 -> rung 1, .7-.85 -> rung 2, .85-.95 -> rung 3, > .95 -> rung 4+.
- Soft vs hard failover: prefer soft (downgrade model variant in same region) before hard (cross-region). Soft failover preserves latency and avoids egress/replication costs.
- Regional affinity window: keep sticky routing for N tokens/requests when switching rungs to prevent thrashing; sticky TTL = 30s by default adjustable per client.
- Quorum protection: control-plane refrains from promoting a higher rung if model-health signals have low quorum (insufficient telemetry) to avoid false positives.

Tiered capacity semantics (Reserved vs Best-effort)
- Reserved pools (Dedicated): guaranteed capacity for specific customers or tiers, not eligible for overflow unless allowed in contract.
- Shared pools (Burst): can be throttled and queued; eligible for ladder steps including regional overflow.
- Emergency pool: small cross-region fast-path for critical customers when primary is down (audit + throttles applied).

Model-variant management patterns
- Model families must carry metadata: quality-estimate, expected latency profile by seq-length, quantization compatibility tag, memory footprint. This metadata drives rung selection.
- Precompute degradation deltas: for each variant pair (A->B) we store expected token-delta, latency reduction %, and eval-score delta so the control-plane can reason about cost vs quality.
- Canary rollouts: allow controlled promotion of a lower-quality variant during load tests to verify user-visible regression thresholds.

Regional overflow policy (avoid thundering cross-region)
- Spill radius: prefer immediate sibling within same cloud region group (e.g., us-west-1 -> us-west-2) before intercontinental. Limit cross-region egress by policy caps.
- Backpressure propagation: when a region signals overflow, sibling regions reduce acceptance rate for new local traffic to avoid replicating overload.
- Egress cost guardrails: for non-enterprise customers, limit cross-region fallback to X requests/min (configurable per org).

Telemetry and SLO alignment
- Telemetry per rung: we must emit rung_id on every trace/span and include model_variant metadata in logs. This makes postmortems tractable.
- Alerting: create separate SLOs per rung mapping. E.g., "Rung1 p99 < 600ms" and a higher-level SLO like ">= 95% requests served at Rung1-2". If distribution drifts outside target, trigger policy shift.
- Quality monitors: automated evals against a core prompt set run every 30m for top variants; model-health scores feed the control-plane.

Operational runbook snippets (for on-call)
- If region capacity alarms fire: 1) verify model-health dashboard for spikes in error/decline, 2) force control-plane to apply rung 2 (prod-distill) for the affected zone, 3) open incident note and annotate with "rung-forced" tag.
- If cross-region egress costs spike unexpectedly: 1) toggle egress caps for non-critical tiers, 2) trigger a rollback to quantized-only for burst traffic, 3) follow-up with cost analysis.
- If incorrect degradations observed (user-reported quality drop): 1) revert to previous rung via control-plane override, 2) run offline eval on sample requests to detect regression, 3) create action item for model owners.

Testing & verification
- Chaos tests: simulate imbalanced region capacity and validate that ladder transitions are monotonic and that traffic stickiness prevents oscillation.
- Load curves: measure latency & cost per rung across realistic seq lengths and prompt complexity; maintain a small matrix that feeds into the precompute metadata.
- Regression harness: tie a canary evaluation set to every model-variant; degradation should not drop below predefined thresholds without a human-approved change.

Open questions / tradeoffs (notes)
- How much per-customer customization? Fine-grained per-org ladder is powerful but increases policy complexity and operational risk. Proposal: default ladder global, allow opt-in custom ladders for enterprise contracts.
- Async degraded responses UX: how do we surface and bill for queued results? Might need a separate API path + SLA semantics.
- Billing alignment: customers should be able to understand cost/quality tradeoffs when we route to a quantized or cached response. Need clear instrumentation in billing pipes.

Next steps / immediate work items
- Spike: implement a policy simulator that consumes real traffic traces and applies ladder logic to quantify SLO reachability. Owner: Mateo. ETA: 3 weeks.
- Metadata hygiene: add variant metadata schema and enforce it on model onboarding. Owner: Jing. ETA: 2 weeks.
- Small chaos run in staging to validate sticky TTL heuristics and prevent thrash. Owner: Ethan. ETA: 4 weeks.

Notes to self / TODOs
- Add example policy JSON block with score thresholds and per-customer overrides (WIP).
- Discuss egress caps with finance to set sane defaults.
- Confirm canary evaluation cadence with applied-ml.

References
- Related runbooks: CONFLUENCE: Cascade Degrade Notes (linked above).
- Jira: PLAT-4821 (policy engine ext), PLAT-4908 (variants metadata).

End of draft — aim to convert to a more formal playbook after the simulator results come back.
